Death Stranding was my personal Game of the Year 2019. I've completed it to 100% on almost every platform (Steam, PS4, Xbox) it's has been released on. Only exception is PS5, since I don't own one.

I absolutely love this game and consider it one of the most unique gaming experiences ever made. The world, the incredible path optimization, the emotional story, and Kojima's signature weirdness come together to create something unlike anything else.

Calling Death Stranding a "walking simulator" or a "delivery simulator" completely misses what the game actually is. Deliveries are only the foundation. The real experience is about rebuilding a broken world, connecting people, overcoming harsh environments, and helping other players through one of the most original asynchronous multiplayer systems ever created. Seeing bridges, roads, ladders, and other structures built by strangers appear in your world (and knowing your own creations are helping someone else) is still a brilliant concept.

The game isn't perfect. Vehicles can behave strangely on rough terrain, and earning every achievement requires a significant amount of grinding. Still, none of that takes away from what makes Death Stranding so special.

It isn't a game for everyone, but if it clicks with you, it becomes an unforgettable experience.

Pros:

+ One of the most original games ever made
+ Fantastic story and memorable world
+ Brilliant asynchronous online system
+ Relaxing yet engaging gameplay loop
+ Outstanding soundtrack and atmosphere
+ Incredible sense of exploration

Cons:

- Vehicles can behave awkwardly
- 100% completion requires a lot of grinding
- Slow pacing isn't for everyone
- Some gameplay systems take time to appreciate

*Death Stranding* is one of the most special games I have ever played. At first, it sounds strange, almost boring: you are Sam Porter Bridges, carrying packages across a broken America. You climb mountains, cross rivers, avoid BTs, repair your boots, balance your cargo, and connect isolated cities to the Chiral Network. But after playing it for a while, I realized the walking was never empty. Every step had weight.

The world feels lonely in a way very few games can capture. You walk through black rocks, rain, snow, ruined cities and silent valleys with only Sam’s breathing, footsteps and BB beside you. Sometimes music suddenly starts while you are walking down a mountain, and the whole game becomes strangely emotional. It feels like the world has ended, but someone still has to keep going.

Sam is the perfect main character for this world. He does not want to be touched. He does not want to connect with people. Everyone asks him to reconnect America, but he can barely connect with anyone himself. That makes his journey powerful. He is not a cheerful hero. He is a tired man carrying too much pain, and slowly, through the journey, he learns to care again.

BB, or Lou, is the heart of the game for me. At first, BB seems like equipment, just a tool to detect BTs. But the longer Sam travels with Lou, the harder it becomes to see that baby as a tool. You soothe Lou after danger, check on her, worry when she gets stressed, and slowly feel attached to her. Their bond is built through small moments, not big speeches. By the end, Lou feels like the one thing keeping Sam human.

That is why the ending is so powerful. When Sam is told to take Lou to the incinerator, it feels like the world is asking him to treat her like cargo. But after everything they have been through, he cannot do that. When he takes Lou out of the pod and begs her to live, the game becomes painfully human. After all the talk about extinction, networks, beaches and the future of humanity, the most important thing is just a man trying to save a child he loves.

Cliff’s story also hit me hard. At first, he feels like a nightmare, a ghost soldier chasing BB through war zones. But later you realize he is not a monster. He is a father trying to save his child. When the truth comes out, and you understand his connection to Sam, the whole story becomes much sadder. Sam has not only been carrying Lou; he has also been carrying a forgotten part of himself.

Fragile is another character I really liked. She is wounded by betrayal and Timefall, but she is not broken. Her name is “Fragile,” but she is one of the strongest people in the game. Her connection with Sam feels quiet and painful, like two lonely people recognizing each other’s scars.

What makes *Death Stranding* amazing is that the gameplay and story are saying the same thing. Delivering cargo is not just a mechanic; it is the theme. Every ladder, bridge, generator, road and sign left by another player feels like a small act of kindness from a stranger you will never meet. In a game about loneliness, invisible people help you survive.

I still remember struggling through snow with too much cargo, almost falling every few steps, and then finding a shelter or zipline another player had built. That feeling is hard to describe. It feels like someone reached across the emptiness and said, “I was here too. You can make it.”

*Death Stranding* is strange, slow and not for everyone, but that is also why I love it. It makes walking emotional. It makes helping people meaningful. It turns isolation into gameplay and connection into something you can actually feel.

By the end, Sam reconnects America, but what really matters is that he connects with Lou. That is the heart of the game. A network can cover the whole country, but none of it means anything if people still treat each other like tools.

This game is not just about delivering packages. It is about continuing to walk after the world has fallen apart. It is about strangers helping each other without meeting. It is about a man afraid of touch learning to love a child.

When I think about *Death Stranding*, I do not first remember the combat or the bosses. I remember Sam walking alone through the rain, Lou sleeping on his chest, music playing in the distance, and a mountain still waiting ahead.

[h3]Death Stranding[/h3]

is a fascinating made third-person Action-Adventure Game with some elements of Shooter-Games as also a bit of Horror-Elements, and a well made and voiced-over story with lots of Cutscene.
And of course it’s a Delivery-Simulator as well, no matter which weather or how dangerous it is, the first rule of the Protagonist is, to always deliver the Packages, tied to the theme that this way the Protagonist is re-connecting the world after a catastrophic Event.

And the Game rewards the Player for this effort as every new Location added to a Network, called the UCA, will provide new Informations and sometimes new Tools that can be crafted and used in order to have different ways of delivering the Packages.
And the Main-Story ties everything nicely together with lots of well made Cutscenes that could easily be adapted into a Movie.

The Game’s strength is its Delivery-Simulator Part in which it gives the Players a lot of Freedom on how to approach each Delivery-Mission, and with each new Tool a new way to solve Problems. And each unlock motivates to unlock even more to see, more to find, more to explore.
And as already mentioned, the cutscenes, well designed Characters, well animated and well spoken Dialoques that give the entire Game a very good Atmosphere, and it has a lot of that stuff in it.
Each new Connection, a new Character, a new Story to discover.

But there are also a few bad things about this Game that need to be mentioned, like when the Character is running (Controller) he sometimes behaves like he tries to defy the Input, ignoring sometimes the direction the joystick is pressed, or even not pressed and he is still running, or moving into another direction and then slip and falls over, damaging the cargo by the Character’s and not the Player’s fault.
Also the Vehicles in the Game have tires that are qualitatively spoken, terrible, in a Game that is so much about Delivery it would have been expected that the Vehicles would have a better grip when driving around the Environment instead of sliding down a hill like a Sled on snow.
And also the Locations added to the Network, the last few where difficult to max out, due to the Game not telling where to find the Missions aimed specifically for said Locations.

Still, this Game is good and I recommend it to Players who enjoy an action-Adventure with Horror-Elements that is focused a lot about bringing Cargo from a to b over dangerous routes as best as possible.
---------------------------------
[h3]Points i give this Game (average Points 7,01 / 10):[/h3]
8,4 / 10 Graphic (Old Game, but the Graphics where it is important is still holding up even today)
9 / 10 Art-Style (The Design of the Monsters and the Human-Enemies are well made and really make them shine as looking threatening)
7,5 / 10 Atmosphere (The Atmosphere is well made in the Areas where it counts, the only Problem there is tho that some sections on long routes can be a bit uneventfull)
8 / 10 Gameplay (Enjoyable Gameplay if Player is into Delivery-Simulator of course)
9,2 / 10 Main-Story (Definitly well made Story and could easily work for a good Movie, even a Franchise. By all the actors they used for motion tracking I wondering why they have not done that.)
7,2 / 10 Side-Story (Each Location is kinda a Side-Story, but after having their Trust maxed out feels kinda like out-of-the-picture, would have been nice to have a bit more involvement of those Side-Characters in the Main-Part)
9 / 10 Characters (Lots of well written and voiced Characters, and the Animations show that the Developers made great use of Motion-Capturing and of course Talent of actual Actors which makes them feel like real Humans would or at least could behave in such Situations)
5 / 10 Soundtrack (They have a lot of licenced Music in it, which was not a bad selected collection, but when it comes to the actual Soundtracks for Combat-Situations against Monsters and Enemies, that Part was not really giving much, could have been better there.)
9,5 / 10 Performance (Game was running well on high settings, only one crash I had during the entire Playthrough)
6,4 / 10 Content (For a Delivery-Simulation with just a few bits of Combat the Content works fine, but the variety of Mission-Types, so it would force the Player to use more different approaches could have been better)
3 / 10 Small-Bugs (There where Moments where the Character seems to do his own thing, which sometimes lead to him falling and damaging the cargo, like running into the wrong direction, or running without input and not stoping, or just those annoying moments when he stops running to look over his shoulders. And of course the constant getting stuck with a Vehicle when driving offroad on small rocks)
4 / 10 Multiplayer (sort of, it allows to use Vehicles and Structures from other Players, but because it picks those randomly and then from Players who placed theirs randomly, more than just once the structures or vehicles where blocking stuff than being helpful)
7 / 10 Online vs. Offline Mode (Offline works much better, in my opinion, but to keep maintaining all the structures, specifically the roads, can be a bit annoying after a while)
8 / 10 Enemies (On higher Difficulty-Levels the Enemies where definitely a nice challenge and even felt like they tried to make use of the Environment, still could be improved on how they would set up the traps for the next encounter with the Player)
4 / 10 Bossfights (The Bossfights are a weakpoint, sure their Design and introduction was nice, but the fight itself was mostly running around and trying to get their healthbar down than anything else, and then there was the end part where at one Bossfight the Game took away all my stuff and forced me to fight with a Rope only, and at another Part of the Game, not allowing me to craft any Tools at all, which felt like the Game changed from one Style to another without warning.)
The game sucks, but it has a beautiful story and runs great on Linux. [Shrug]

Some people will glance at this game and see it as a walking simulator where the main character is the mailman chugging energy drinks.

Some manage to see past that first obvious layer and see the beauty underneath it. The relaxing sensations of walking a mountain while absorbing the stunning visuals and the tasteful soundtrack. 

Then you start seeing the game for what it truly is. A neo-social interactive experience. Neither a multiplayer game nor a single player. One where your actions and decisions can influence others, if they let you to. One where you can lay a helping hand to a faceless stranger, just for the sake of doing the helping. And be helped just the same, if you let yourself be helped.

Last but not least, its probably one of the fastest loading games I've experienced. The optimization is truly asian-level.

It had a lot of potential though, the graphics are insanely good, the Actors that he introduced to the game are all great, and although kind of a boring walking simulator, if he managed to add more interesting things to do, a better combat system and an actual story that has any resemblance to something that make at least some sense we would have a new cool franchise. 

But all my hopes went down the same putrid stinky human waste pipe that the game belongs to.
Death Stranding 2 is a fever dream of a guy that wanted to be a Film maker instead of a game developer, too bad he has no talent in that.

The story is a mishmash of random texts and cutscenes that add absolutely nothing to character development, making me wonder if the story of this game was made by an actual human, because it sounds like it was made by SLOP A.I.

The gameplay is as boring as the first one, the "challenge" and "dangers" in the game is so easy to bypass as long as you have the patience to use the corners of the map. The boss fights are so incredibly underwhelming, from the cool boss fights we had on the metal gear series, to the most basic and boring ways to finish a boss on both this trashy games.

I could go on and on why the second game is a piece of trash,  but it all comes down to:

It’s obvious that Death Stranding is a game that will strongly divide players.
You’ll either be among those who feel annoyed and bored by the gameplay, or among those who take a simple kind of pleasure from it. Judging by the fact that I recommend it, you’ve probably guessed it already: I’m part of the second group.
That said, I’ll play devil’s advocate (to some extent): yes, it’s slow and yes, it can feel a bit repetitive. As for the slow, methodical aspect, it’s clearly intentional, and I never found the game frustrating. It’s not even that laborious, really—proof of that is that I never died in the game (at least during my open-world deliveries), and I didn’t fail a single delivery.
Repetitive? Not that much, since you don’t spend the entire game in the same areas and you unlock tools that make your job easier. In fact, repetitive or not, I found the world so beautiful and immersive that I never got tired of going back and forth and exploring these stunning landscapes—it’s extremely relaxing to me.
On top of that, one thing that really kept me invested in the game was this strong sense of contribution. First with the NPCs, with whom you can improve your reputation and unlock new things, but above all with other players. I take immense pleasure in building structures and knowing that they helped other players. And it works both ways: I feel a real sense of gratitude when I come across something left behind by another player that ends up helping me. I’ve never enjoyed the feeling of cooperation in a game as much as I did here—even though it’s technically a single-player game where you never directly meet anyone else.
As for the story, I think it’s incredible. We all thought “WTF” when we saw the first trailers, and yet everything ends up being very understandable and fairly coherent. It’s incredibly original. I tip my hat to Kojima for daring to go off the beaten path and letting his creativity run free. I think many of us are happy to play as Norman Reedus, but honestly, all the characters are outstanding.
In short, whether you like the game or not will depend entirely on you and your personal tastes. It’s not a game I would recommend to everyone, but for me, it was a massive slap in the face. In fact, I don’t even have a point of comparison to say “if you like X, then play Death Stranding”—the game is just that unique.

This game.. was one of the most unique experiences I've had so far while playing.
The story of the game revolves around the world of the dead colliding with the one of the living, triggering a Death Stranding. A world where a person dying is one of the biggest risks: after death, if the body necrotizes, they turn into a BT, and too many BT's in one location cause a voidout, a big explosion that wipes an astonishing portion of the earth where it triggers, leaving a crater of tar.
You play as Sam, a "porter", the backbone of society, the couriers that go through the wasteland and through the rapidly-aging rain called Timefall. So basically the game feels like a FedEx simulator, delivering packages to settlements all over the map.
There are two main dangers along the way: BT's and human enemies. BT's are self explainatory, while the human enemies are of two types: MULE's and terrorists. While MULE's have an unhealthy obsession for stealing packages, their tactics are non-lethal, whereas the terrorists are just hell-bent on wreaking havoc wherever they set camp.
Progressing through the story, you get different kinds of weapons to fight back both BT's and humans. But beware! To avoid "contributing" to the already bad situation, and creating more BT's by killing other humans, against them, non-lethal tactics are usually the way to go, either with non-lethal ammunition weapons, or the BOLA gun, a really fun weapon that shoots a lasso that ties your enemy up, leaving you to only give it a kick to stun him and prevent him from waking up for a while. 
Because you are human, if you get a hefty load, you can't carry it all on your back, and with that, you get to unlock different means of help: carriers, bikes and trucks. the 2nd portion of the map also has distributed spots where you can rebuild a highway, which is a game changer because of the dangerous terrain, which makes it impossible to travel with a vehicle. 
The story builds up good around the 2nd part of the game, on the 2nd part of the map, that is huge, and three of my favorite moments were the storms that transport you to a combat veteran's "Beach"(a land where the dead dwell), which cover three significant events: World War I. World war II and the war in Vietnam, where you can roam around and are the most action packed portions of the game, while BT and human encounters can easily be avoided if you manage to detour their areas. 
So, one of the biggest disclaimers I can make is: The first few hours are the toughest ones to go through, where you literally have to walk from place to place. Once you start to get your first bike, first equipments and start rebuilding the roads.. the game will feel way more fun! 
So I really recommend this game if you have the time, and your attention span can handle a different kind of pace in a game.

(Like when I said "The Onion", was I subliminally referring to the joke-news website, reinforcing the idea that this entire review is a self-aware joke? Or was it unintentional? I played this game while using my mommy's lap as a gaming chair, and while she said that she didn't [i]get[/i] Death Stranding, I could tell by the gleam in her eyes that she had a good time by modern gaming standards. Clifford the Big Red Dog is referenced to in this game, and I love that! Death Stranding is, first and foremost, a game by Hideo Kojima.  That alone says a lot.  At times it borders on being an interactive movie with a very nuanced story that will leave you with plenty to think about when the game is over.  I played this game on two different systems, so my experiences are subjective and based solely on how the game looked and ran on my systems.  Here are the specs of those systems so that you can gauge for yourself how it may run for you.

System 1: Steam Deck
Resolution was set to 720p and graphics quality was set to "default", except I disabled motion blur and anti-aliasing because, in my opinion, on the handheld screen AA is unnecessary, and when docked on my TV, the jagged edges were less distracting than the fuzziness introduced by trying to AA a 720p image that's being blown up onto a 55 inch 4k display.

System 2
CPU: AMD FX 8370 (stock clock speeds, 4.0 Ghz)
GPU: AMD Radeon RX 480 8GB (Overclocked "Gaming" edition from MSI)
RAM: 16GB DDR3 1866
OS: Debian GNU/Linux Bookworm ("Testing" at time of play-through)
Resolution was set to 1080p and graphics quality was set to its highest preset and the game consistently held 60+ fps with very occasional dips into the 50s, particularly when traveling fast through the world on something like a motorcycle.

[h1]Graphics and Visual Design[/h1]
The graphics for the game are absolutely top notch.  One particularly impressive feature of the game's graphics are the character faces and animations.  It's obvious that the characters were generated using some kind of facial scanning, but they've managed to achieve a very high level of detail so that the character models look incredibly realistic, without producing an eery "uncanny valley" type of feeling when you see them animated in the context of a video game.  The particle effects, object and character models, the creatures, the terrain, everything about this game just looks amazing in terms of artistic quality and style.  If you're worried about the first game from Kojima Productions lacking in the visual department, then don't, because in terms of graphics, the game looks amazing.  There were plenty of times that it was hard to believe that the cutscenes were all running in-engine and weren't pre-rendered.

The developers also did a wonderful job using the graphics to convey information about the world you're in.  For example, the tape on packages you're carrying will flash to indicate if a package is sustaining damage.  Highways that can be rebuilt in the game will eventually degrade over time, and the appearance of the road will change as it degrades so that you have a visual clue as to the condition of the road without actually having to go check what its exact remaining durability is.  Even Sam's "life" gauge only appears when you're actually in combat, and even then, it floats in the air next to him instead of taking up permanent real estate on your screen somewhere.

My only complaint visually is that the "cities" don't feel very "city" like.  Concept art portrayed sprawling walled in cities, but all you really see in the game is a delivery center where you drop packages, and most people in the game speak to you remotely via a hologram.  The world is big "enough", but there's a little bit of a disconnect in terms of scale between what you see and what is stated by the plot.

[h1]Audio[/h1]
The musical score for the game is wonderful.  There is a whole set of original music used as background music for the game's environments, but there's also a lot of licensed music tracks from the band "Low Roar" that is commonly used as the backdrop for important moments in the story, and it does a really good job of both bringing visibility to a band I had never heard of, while also setting the mood for whatever is going on at that particular moment.

The sound design in terms of environmental sound effects is also really well executed.  The enemies in the game are invisible to the naked eye most of the time except under specific circumstances, but you can still make use of directional audio (easier with headphones) to pinpoint the location of enemies.  The game also makes really good use audio cues.  There are sound effects for when you receive "likes" from other players and special sound effects for all kinds of things to convey information to the player without being loud and obnoxious.

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]
The main gameplay loop is delivering packages.  You'll pick up a package at one place, be asked to deliver it to a new place, and along the ways probably have to avoid or engage with some enemies.  The package may have some special requirements such as not getting it wet, keeping it held level, getting it there in a certain amount of time, etc, and when you get to the delivery point there will be some sort of story progression, a cutscene or a boss fight of some kind, followed by another delivery task.  It's weird, but at first I didn't think I would enjoy the game as much as I did.  I bought it solely because it was from Hideo Kojima.  But to be completely honest, I've found the game to be a lot more addicting than I was expecting.  There's always something you're wanting to do such as leveling up your relationship with a particular person, building more roads or other facilities to make future deliveries easier, searching for hidden items, reading mail messages from, or interviews of various characters in the game to fill in the plot, etc.

The primary enemies of the game (BTs) were, for me, extremely intimidating at first.  They absolutely scared the pants off me.  But, as you progress, not only do you unlock equipment and upgrades to make delivering packages easier, but you unlock better weapons and items to deal with the enemies you face in the game.  The combat can actually be very satisfying, but being a Kojima game, there are consequences to everything you do.  Dealing with "enemies" in certain ways can be rewarding, and dealing with them in other ways can actually lead to more headache.

One of the coolest features of the game is the passive online multiplayer.  If you enable the online feature in the settings, the game connects you with other players.  You will never actually see one another in game, but once certain requirements are met in each region, you will be able to see and interact with signs, structures and vehicles left by other players, and they yours.  It makes the world feel much less empty.

[h1]Story[/h1]
This is a Hideo Kojima game.  You play it primarily for the story, for the nuance and world building and character development, and this game definitely delivers.  You are Sam Bridges, a delivery man, a porter.  In a post apocalyptic world where it's dangerous to go out in the open and the worlds of the living and the dead are not completely separate any more, people have withdrawn into their own bunkers or into enclosed and protected cities, and it's your job, along with countless other porters, to deliver the items necessary to help keep people alive and society functioning.  But, the end is near, and some would rather see it sooner than later, and it falls to you to protect the future of humanity in a world that's barely hanging on as it is.  It's a deep, nuanced, sometimes confusing narrative, but it's interesting and exciting, and sometimes confusing all at once.  It is indeed a Kojima production.

[h1]Summary[/h1]
While I would have liked to see the cities and the country fleshed out a bit more, overall, I thoroughly enjoyed Kojima Productions' first game.  It's a wonderful, beautiful, detailed experience with a lot to discover, and a strangely addicting gameplay loop that will keep you coming back even after you've finished the main story.  If you're a fan of his past work with Metal Gear, I highly recommend you try out Death Stranding.  It looks like we may be in for another grand adventure if he continues this story in future games, and I'm excited to see what comes next.

Death Stranding is an indie game with triple-A scope and polish. An absolute masterpiece that happily ignores what is a blockbuster and what sells the most to do its own thing.

In this practically sandbox game the focus is traversal. You will be delivering packages and worrying about terrain, routes, equipment, tools, dangers and cargo load. The landscape around you is desolate, composed of a vast stretches of land where rivers, mountains, gravel or weather are not just cosmetic, but an active worry you  have to plan against.
The world is mysterious, with an intriguing and extremely original concept Why does rain age people so fast? What are the invisible creatures that kill people? What is the Death Stranding? The game lets your curiosity be the pulling force moving you forward, but always at your own leisure.

Don't be fooled by Kojima's reputation: this is not a MGS4 cutscene-fest where you go through a linear level only to be greeted by lengthy cinematics. Sure, this game has his fair share of cutscenes at the beggining, and ends with a couple hours worth of almost kabuki levels of acting - a Kojima's hallmark we do still get -, but the body of the game is almost sandbox on its aproach. In a sense, this is much closer to the design philosophy of MGS5.

And that's why I would recommend this game, even if you end up not liking it: In a time where big-budget games are almost clones of one another, playing to the safest card, designed by comittee, here comes Kojima - of all people - to remind us that videogames, as a medium, is largely unexplored yet. We shouldn't confine ourselves to play the same game over and over just because it is bussiness safe for companies. Everyone should at least try this game, if only to see what is possible.

I think Death Stranding was my favourite game of 2019 but I understand why it divided people so much. It's definitely not a game for everyone, you really have to gel with its gameplay loop. You're going to be doing a lot of walking so at the end of the day you're going to need some level of patience and the ability to immerse yourself in the game world. The story and characters knocked it out of the park for me but that's another very subjective thing. I think you need to have a certain way of thinking to really get into the challenge of the gameplay. Planning perfect routes, using the correct tools, know how to deal with the various crazy situations you'll run into. It all appeals to certain people. Also a big factor of my enjoyment that I can see becoming a problem down the track is the online component. It's simply amazing to see a player based infrastructure just build itself slowly as you play the game. Routes that were once tricky or annoying now easily traversed thank to the ingenuity of other players and yourself combined. Without that my enjoyment would have been severely lessened. That said you're still looking at a fantastic game all in all and it's a big recommend from me

Maxed and 500L'd this game, loved the cinematics, loved the different play modes, I even enjoyed the third person shooter dynamic though yeah the combat became less about enjoying combat, and more about satisfyingly clearing out an area for "some time" by knocking the humans out, or snipping BTs.

I went all in on developing the road and zipline networks, ending up with mostly well-maintained L3 zips; the scarcity of chemicals and sometimes chiral crystals did make this an interesting non-core, non-side-quest, non-relevant, but immensely rewarding completionist part of the game. Why drive for 20 minutes when you can zipline for 10?

Meta-game-play tip: Once you complete the game, prop your phone nearby and max Legend deliveries (or LOL) to 500 (w/sound off) while watching Whitelight's 7 hour review.

You'll get to nod your head at the critiques of BT combat, but more importantly, relive the moments you loved/liked (personal: someone hugging "themself" -- so scifi-personal I love it).

And after that, watch some No More Bikes and wonder why Death Stranding is a Walking Game With No Sidewalks!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!

My gripes:
BT combat yeah, but also, why not let me clear an area and then have the sun come out?
That slippery front-end of the van.
Chemicals shortage all the time for a L3 zipline network.
Ziplines don't auto-like so I never knew if anyone used my mountain peak zips -- crucial lack of likes there.
The L/LOL 500 orders compelled my completionist compulsion.
Yeah, yeah, some of the plot/logic holes, but they never derailed me.

Final note: Much of this game is about completing jobs and building things that others can use, and both of those things are just.... SATISFYING.

Death Stranding is quite seriously a game unlike anything the industry has ever seen. I have never been a fanboy of Kojima, I haven't even played any of his previous games, but for his debut Kojima has absolutely smashed his way into the scene like a wrecking ball. Death Stranding is honestly an enigma, despite how fleshed out its lore and world is. It's an anomaly amongst the plethora of tired, cookie cutter, rinse+repeat formulaic games that the industry is absolutely inundated with these days. 

Everything about the game feels overwhelmingly raw and organic, from its visual presentation, its musical score and accompanying soundtrack, its core gameplay loop. How the barren and harsh landscape mottled with misshapen rock, winding rivers and creeks conflicts but blends perfectly with the almost brutalist and monolithic architecture, that serves as the only remnants of humanity feels almost akin to the cinematography of Prometheus and Covenant. I've never played a game that felt so believable and grounded despite its futuristic premises. From the tiniest, most crucial design details in paraphernalia, to the complete function of movement, to the most intrinsic attention to detail in the environment and seemingly most mundane things. Death Standing isn't just a breath of fresh air, it's almost a cultural shock to what we expect from the quality, and potential of videogames.

I dare say that if this games opening sequence doesn't intrigue you, you will be hard pressed to devote any further time beyond it, but should you persist into the further and beyond, the game will eventually open up to one of the most mechanically sound and robust experiences you can pinpoint to within - I daresay - the last decade.

From a gameplay perspective, Death Stranding is a highly elaborate and complex 'walking simulator' with strong courier elements. The core gameplay revolves around making deliveries to various clients in the most efficient way possible. The contents aren't so much as important, but rather, the reasoning behind it. DS however ramps everything up to the Nth degree, you will have to consider the terrain, angles of slopes, obstacles, potential hostiles, and even harsh elements that degrade or potentially damage the quality of the packages. In all instances you must consider weight, and in some, you must even consider vibration and alignment. Combat is present but features both lethal, and non-lethal means of engaging in it. This will drastically impact your route choices as the risk of cargo being damaged increases with the distance typically travelled. The games features are fully fleshed out when you play connected online, wherein joint worlds will allow you to see and interact with other players objects and structures to help you navigate the bleak and lifeless landscape. You can even see the roads most travelled as surfaces blotch and erode due to wear and tear. You are adamantly encouraged to participate in this ritual by contributing to the community in more ways than one. I have never seen a game before that features and so strongly emphasises a philosophical, physical, and spiritual significance in its own constructed society.

Story wise, this game blew everyone away with its reveal trailer and sparked heightened amounts of curiosity, awe and wonderment. This game completely lived up to the expectations it set, and even more. I was utterly dumbstruck and confounded at what I had witnessed, and every cutscene further beckoned me to divulge in its zaniness and intrigue. I surrendered myself completely to the unknown and emerged on the other side having experienced something like no other. I will - no I MUST reiterate, that Kojima absolutely obliterated his way into the industry with this game. This game will weird you out, it will gross you out, it will elate you, it will destroy you. You will experience fear, shock, terror, dread, wonderment, bewilderment, you will be inspired, enlightened, intrigued, and all that lies in between. To speak any further of the story, is to rob it of its chance to amaze you.

Musically this game is an absolute treat. The original score is a hybrid blend of techno and synth with vocal orchestra and strings. It covers a range of facets and emotions as it drives the story and environment home with pieces that feel adventurous, tense, powerful, uplifting, and heartwrenching. To accompany the score is a soundtrack handpicked by Kojima himself, featuring bands like - predominantly - Low Roar, Silent Poets, and CHVRCHES. Typically the band pieces play in select narrative instances where they help to establish and ground a set of emotions. The way music is utilised in this game oozes authenticity, and permeates a level of creativity and ingenuity reminiscent of some of the best directed movies. There were very few musical sequences that weren't tantalising to say the least. 

In conclusion, I fully believe that Death Stranding offers an experience like no other. There may be some familiar or similar elements to other franchises, but Kojima has managed to make his mark upon the gaming world, and we are all enriched for it. Death Stranding is truly a passion project, born from the fruits of long and arduous labour, and sweetened by the trials and tribulations of past events long, and only recently transpired. This game left me wanting more, it left me fulfilled enough to feel confident in what I've been left with, but it left me eager and excited to see what the future has in store for this new IP. 

Kudos to Kojima and team, for bringing to me an experience so profound and rewarding, I'll never forget it.

I bought this game for the story and overall experience, and it sorely disappointed there. "Subtlety" isn't an even remotely understood concept by whoever was on the narrative team. The game will constantly nag you and lampshade concepts that you got the first five times they were explained. Characters just cannot shut up for the first dozen hours and almost made me drop the game right there and then. Meanwhile, trainwrecks of cutscene marathons interspaced with time-wasting gameplay are plenty. They were the final straw for me.

The narrative keeps hinting at some big secrets and reveals but never delivers on them. The story is hollow and on the nose, every theme and idea ones you could already glimpse from a distance. This is pretty much all there is to it, with a few ideas stretched far beyond their value. What few plot twists there are are so badly-executed and meaningless that I couldn't bring myself to care by the time they happened.

The best parts of the game are actually those where it lets itself be played without any sort of narration getting in the way. Even then, it's pretty basic and I wouldn't recommend it at anything approaching full price. The online component is opaque but well realized and I do think that this collaborative aspect is perhaps the game's strongest suit. It still does fall on its face with movement physics that feel very frustrating and unpredictable at the worst times, which is a fatal flaw for a hiking simulator.

This review would have been a little more positive if the game had had less frustrating game mechanics and blatant disrespect for the player's time on top of those problems. Having finished the game, I can't say that I really feel happy with my purchase even with a sizeable discount.

YMMV but if you are on the fence with Kojima stories as I was, well, I'd recommend you stay behind it until the cost of entry is ankle-high. It's really not that good and, to be honest, rather pretentious.
